scenes.name: Hardcore en la era del punk-pop: emocore, ska-core y post-hardcore
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Mientras las revistas anuncian la «muerte del punk», el hardcore se convierte en un movimiento que no deja pueblo sin tocar y genera subgéneros. El «emocore» (Jawbreaker, Weezer, Sunny Day Real Estate, Promise Ring, At The Drive-In, Jimmy Eat World, Seaweed); el hardcore progresivo de Washington (Nation Of Ulysses, Make-Up, Shudder To Think, Jawbox, Edsel, Lungfish, Circus Lupus, Dismemberment Plan); el «ska-core» (Operation Ivy, Rancid, Mighty Mighty Bosstones, Sublime, No Doubt); el punk-pop que llega a las listas (Green Day, Offspring, Flop, Pennywise, Pegboy, Superchunk, Queers); el garage-punk californiano (Drive Like Jehu, Rocket From The Crypt, Blink 182, Zen Guerrilla); el jazzcore (Bazooka, Iceburn); la vieja escuela (D Generation, Supersuckers, Zeke, Dropkick Murphys, Silverfish, Turbonegro) y el post-hardcore de Unwound.

podcast.title: Formation and Name Change (1992-1994)
podcast.body: The band formed in 1992 outside San Diego, initially named "Blink." They later changed their name to "Blink 182" in 1994 due to a legal issue with another band in Ireland. "Blink 182 forms in 1992 outside of San Diego."

podcast.title: Early Warped Tour Appearance (1996)
podcast.body: In 1996, Blink-182 was just one of many emerging bands on the Warped Tour, described as "just another face in the crowd." "And at that time, they were just another face in the crowd, one of more than a dozen new bands being given a chance to show their stuff."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Return for 1997 Tour
podcast.body: Blink-182 was among the bands that returned to participate in the Warped Tour in 1997. "Like 1 and 2 was back, as were the boss tones."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: 24 Years of the Warped Tour

podcast.title: Band Fracturing (2004)
podcast.body: The band began to fracture during a tense tour with No Doubt in 2004, leading to internal conflicts. "After a good run in tens of millions of albums, Blink 182 started to fracture."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: The Dollar Bill Tour (2004)
podcast.body: The tour following the release of the self-titled album began with an All Ages Club Tour, where tickets were sold for $8, and included a golden ticket contest for a private concert. The tour ran throughout 2004, concluding in Dublin on December 16th, with a planned 2005 leg ultimately canceled due to renewed internal tensions. "The tour that followed the release of the fifth album was called The Dollar Bill Tour."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 2

podcast.title: Tom's Demand for Hiatus (2004)
podcast.body: At the end of the No Doubt tour, Tom decided he "didn't need this crap anymore" and demanded six months off, citing a need for more family time, which was problematic given a major US tour and charity event commitments. "At the end of that no doubt tour, Tom decided he didn't need this crap anymore. He demanded six months off. I need more time with my family, he said."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Tom's Health and Addiction Issues (2004-2005)
podcast.body: Tom suffered from severe back pain, which led to an addiction to prescription painkillers. "Meanwhile, Tom's back was bad, really bad, and this led to an addiction to prescription pain killers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Hiatus and Internal Conflicts (2005)
podcast.body: In February 2005, Blink-182 announced an official hiatus, which was effectively a breakup due to widespread fatigue and interpersonal friction among the members after nearly a decade of intense work. The band had transitioned from being teenagers to adults, leading to personal changes and a desire to pursue individual paths. The record label, despite the internal issues, strictly instructed the band not to publicly state that it was the end of the band. "Part two of the Blink 182 story ended with the announcement of the hiatus in February 2005."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 3

podcast.title: Indefinite Hiatus (2005)
podcast.body: An indefinite hiatus was announced on February 22nd, 2005, following a period of uncertainty and internal friction, during which Tom DeLonge and Mark Hoppus ceased communication for years. "Things got to the point where they couldn't continue, and an indefinite hiatus was announced on February 22nd, 2005."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up with Blink 182

podcast.title: Indefinite Hiatus and Breakup (2005)
podcast.body: Over Christmas 2004, old tensions resurfaced, leading to a breakdown in communication among band members. On February 22, 2005, management announced an "indefinite hiatus." The statement explained the band's need for time with loved ones after over a decade of non-stop work. However, this was effectively a breakup, initiated when Tom DeLonge's demand for a six-month break was deemed too long by Mark and Travis, leading to Tom quitting the band. "On February 22, 2005, announcing that the group was going on, quote, indefinite hiatus."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 2

podcast.title: Tom Quits (February 22, 2005)
podcast.body: The internal issues culminated on this date when Tom called the manager and declared, "I quit!" "Everything finally blew up on February 22nd 2005. Tom called the manager and said, I quit!"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Decision to Reunite (Late 2008)
podcast.body: Following these events, the band members began talking and collectively decided it was "time to put the band back together." "Anyway, bottom line is that everyone got back together, started talking and decided that yeah, you know what, it was time to put the band back together."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Hospital Reunion (2008)
podcast.body: Following Travis Barker's severe injuries from the plane crash, Mark Hoppus was among the first to visit him in the hospital, and Tom Delonge also made the trip. The three members of Blink-182 met in a "sobering reunion" at Travis's bedside, prompting a realization for all three about what truly mattered in their lives and relationships. "The three guys met up in the hospital in a pretty sobering reunion."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 3

podcast.title: Jerry Finn's Death (2008)
podcast.body: The sudden death of their long-time producer Jerry Finn in 2008, coupled with Travis Barker's near-fatal plane crash, "shocked everyone back to reality" and helped the band members sort out their issues, leading to their eventual reunion. "along with drummer Travis Barker's near fatal plane crash and the sudden death of their long-time producer Jerry Flynn, both in 2008. That shocked everyone back to reality and things got sorted out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up with Blink 182

podcast.title: Producer Jerry Finn's Death (August 2008)
podcast.body: The death of their longtime producer, Jerry Finn, from a cerebral hemorrhage in August 2008 brought the band members together at his funeral, prompting introspection and "self-examination about life at the universe and everything." "Second, their longtime producer, Jerry Finn, died of a cerebral hemorrhage in August of 2008. That brought everybody together at the funeral where the usual sort of self-examination about life at the universe and everything happened."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Reunion Triggered by Plane Crash (2008)
podcast.body: One of the positive outcomes of drummer Travis Barker's near-fatal plane crash on September 19, 2008, was that it served as a catalyst for the reunion of Blink-182. The band subsequently released the album "Neighborhoods" almost three years to the day after the crash. "About the only good thing about the whole incident, other than the fact that Travis lived, is that it spurred the reunion of Blink 182."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Airplanes!

podcast.title: Travis Barker's Plane Crash (2008)
podcast.body: On September 19, 2008, less than a month after Jerry Finn's death, Travis Barker and DJ AM were involved in a Learjet 60 plane crash in Columbia, South Carolina, after a show. The chartered plane, which Travis was persuaded to take by DJ AM, suffered underinflated tires that burst during takeoff, causing the landing gear to collapse and the plane to crash through lights, a fence, across a highway, and into an embankment. Travis and DJ AM were the only two survivors from the six people on board. "Then came the plane crash. This was September 19th, 2008."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 3

podcast.title: Travis Barker's Plane Crash (September 21, 2008)
podcast.body: Travis and DJ AM were the sole survivors of a private Learjet crash on this date; the plane slammed into a fence on takeoff, exploded, and caught fire. Travis sustained "horrible second and third-degree burns" and required weeks in intensive care, where Tom and Mark visited him, leading to "more soul-searching." "And then third, it got really weird on September 21st 2008 when Travis and his buddy DJ Am were the only two survivors of a jet plane crash."

srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Travis Barker's Plane Crash Survival (2008)
podcast.body: In 2008, blink-182 drummer Travis Barker was the sole survivor of a horrific private jet crash in Columbia, South Carolina. The accident resulted in the death of his friend, DJ AM. "Blink wanted to drummer Travis Barker was the only survivor of a horrendous private jet crash in Columbia, South Carolina in 2008, an accident that killed his friend DJ AM."

podcast.title: Reunion Announced (February 8, 2009)
podcast.body: Three years, 11 months, and 17 days after Tom quit, Blink 182 announced their reunion live on the Grammy Awards. "So on February 8th, 2009, three years, 11 months, and 17 days since Tom said I quit. Blake announced live on the Grammy Awards that they were back together."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Reunion Announcement (2009)
podcast.body: The band officially announced their reunion at the 2009 Grammy Awards. This was followed by a reunion tour during the summer, signaling their return to active music creation and performance. "Their first appearance together was at the 2009 Grammy Awards, where they announced that they were getting back together."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 3

podcast.title: Departure from Interscope Records (2012)
podcast.body: In October 2012, Blink-182 split from their major label, Interscope Records. This move allowed them to pursue independent projects, such as their five-song EP "Dogs Eating Dogs," giving them complete creative control without external interference. "They left Interscope Records in October 2012."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 3

podcast.title: Forced Indie Status (2012)
podcast.body: In October 2012, following the unsatisfactory performance of their album *Neighborhoods*, the band's label severed ties. This forced Blink 182 to become independent, a "pretty demoralizing thing" for a band that had sold tens of millions of albums. "Their label wasn't happy with the performance of Neighborhoods, and in October 2012, the band was cut loose and forced to go indie, a pretty demoralizing thing after selling tens of millions of albums."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up with Blink 182

podcast.title: Resurfacing Internal Issues (Late 2014)
podcast.body: After their album *Dogs Eating Dogs* and more tours, the "old cracks returned" within the band. Issues between Tom DeLonge and Mark Hoppus, coupled with Travis Barker's fear of flying preventing overseas tours, came to a head in late 2014. "There were more tours, but the old cracks returned."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up with Blink 182

podcast.title: Tom DeLonge's Departures (2014-2015)
podcast.body: Tom DeLonge initially quit the band for one day in early 2014 but was persuaded to return. Tensions escalated again in early 2015 when he insisted on recording his parts in San Diego while Mark and Travis worked in LA. A week before studio convergence, Mark and Travis received an email from Tom's manager stating his unwillingness to participate, citing a desire to focus on non-musical projects. Another account suggests he was presented with a 60-page contract demanding sole focus on Blink, which he couldn't accept due to prior commitments. He consequently quit for a second time. "Tensions built, and a week before everyone was supposed to convene in the studio for the final push, Mark and Travis got an email from Tom's manager saying that he no longer wanted to participate in Blink 182."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up with Blink 182

podcast.title: Tom Delonge's Second Departure (2014-2015)
podcast.body: Tom Delonge quit the band again around 2014, although he briefly returned proposing group therapy led by motivational speaker Tony Robbins, which did not resolve underlying issues. Communication ceased once more, leading to indefinite delays for a planned 2013 album. His manager eventually sent an email, one week before a scheduled studio session, stating Tom's indefinite unwillingness to participate in Blink-182 activities. The band issued a statement announcing his departure, to which Tom countered that the band demanded he put all other projects on hold for an album and tour within six months. He refused these terms and officially left. "Tom's manager sent an email... saying that Tom did not want to participate in any Blink activities indefinitely."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 3

podcast.title: Matt Skiba's Recruitment and First Performance (2015)
podcast.body: After Tom DeLonge's second departure, Mark Hoppus and Travis Barker decided against disbanding Blink 182 and recruited Matt Skiba from Alkaline Trio. Their first performance with Skiba on March 18, 2015, marked the first time Mark Hoppus played in Blink without Tom DeLonge, after which Skiba was made an official member. "Mark and Travis had no plans to kill Blink so they brought in Matt Skiba from Alkaline Trio."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up with Blink 182

podcast.title: Max Schieber Joins (2015)
podcast.body: In March 2015, following Tom Delonge's second departure, Blink-182 played two club shows with Max Schieber (likely Matt Skiba) of Alkaline Trio filling in as guitarist. Lawyers worked to formalize Tom's exit and Max's integration into the band. "In March 2015, Blink played two club shows without Tom. Max Schieber, the guitarist for a band called Alkaline Trio filled in."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 3

podcast.title: Fyre Festival Withdrawal (2017)
podcast.body: Just hours before the disastrous Fyre Festival was scheduled to begin on April 28, 2017, Blink-182 announced via Twitter that they were pulling out. The band cited concerns about their ability to deliver a quality performance, implying doubts about payment and the adequacy of production needs for staging, sound, and lights at the festival. "Regrettably, and after much careful and difficult consideration, we want to let you know that we won't be performing at Fire Fest in the Bahamas."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 1: (100-91)

podcast.title: COVID-19 Tour Cancellation (2020)
podcast.body: A significant world tour planned for the *Nine* album was canceled due to the COVID-19 pandemic lockdown in March 2020, likely impacting the album's potential commercial success and preventing them from achieving a desired top 40 hit. "A big tour had been planned but that of course was canceled."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up with Blink 182

podcast.title: Last Show with Matt Skiba (2020)
podcast.body: The band's last live performance before the COVID-19 pandemic, held in Los Angeles on January 18, 2020, also turned out to be the final show featuring Matt Skiba as a member of Blink 182. "Blinks last show before everything hit the fan was in Los Angeles on January 18, 2020. And that also turned out to be the last show with Mads Keeba."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up with Blink 182

podcast.title: Tom DeLonge's Return and Reconciliation (2022)
podcast.body: By mid-2022, rumors of a reunion circulated, leading to the band's social media accounts being wiped in October. On October 11, the official announcement was made that Tom DeLonge was back, and an album and a two-year world tour were planned. This reconciliation was spurred by Mark Hoppus's cancer diagnosis, which prompted Tom to reach out immediately. "And that's when news came down that Mark, Travis and Tom, came to the realization that it was time to bury all the animosities and get back to being Blink 182."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up with Blink 182

podcast.title: Coachella Comeback Performance (2023)
podcast.body: On April 14, 2023, Blink 182 was announced as a surprise replacement headliner for Frank Ocean at Coachella with only two days' notice. This marked the original lineup's (Mark, Travis, Tom) first performance together in nine years (since 2014). They played an hour-long set to an audience of 150,000, which was described as one big sing-along. "In the interim, they got to make a big comeback together at Coachella on April 14th, 2023."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up with Blink 182

podcast.title: Hard Rock and One More Time Tours (2023-2024)
podcast.body: The band embarked on a headline tour, known as the Hard Rock Tour for its first leg and the One More Time Tour for its second. It ran from May 2023 to November 8, 2024, spanning four legs and 91 shows, with each concert featuring approximately 25 songs. This tour achieved the "biggest box office take of any rock tour that year." Three dates were canceled: one due to a hurricane and two for routine illnesses. "The headline tour, known as the Hard Rock Tour and the One More Time Tour for the second leg, began in May 2023 and didn't end until November 8, 2024."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up with Blink 182

podcast.title: Missionary Impossible Tour (2025)
podcast.body: Following their extensive 2023-2024 tours, the band initiated the Missionary Impossible Tour in 2025. This tour was notable for featuring many songs that Blink 182 had not performed in decades. "That was followed by the missionary impossible tour in 2025, which saw the band play a lot of songs that they hadn't touched in decades."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up with Blink 182

podcast.title: Fourth Decade and Resilience (2026)
podcast.body: By 2026, Blink 182 was actively performing and showing no signs of slowing down, entering their fourth decade as a band. Despite numerous past challenges where things threatened to "break down completely," the members consistently managed to pull it back together. "Blink 182 is now into their fourth decade."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up with Blink 182

podcast.title: "Enema of the State" Album Cover Model
podcast.body: The "sexy nurse" on the cover of Blink-182's 1999 album "Enema of the State" is Jeanine Lindemulder, a porn star, though the band was unaware of her profession when they selected her photo from options provided by their record label. Photographer Dave Goldman, who conducted the shoot on March 12, 1999, was also oblivious to both Lindemulder's background and the band's identity. "Well, it's porn star, Jeanine Lindemolder."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Stories Behind Iconic Album Covers Part 2

podcast.title: "Sellout" Backlash from Fans
podcast.body: Upon signing with MCA, a major record label, Blink-182 faced considerable criticism and "an awful lot of grief" from their fanbase, who accused them of being "sellouts" for abandoning their independent punk roots. "But Blink's fans gave them an awful lot of grief for signing with a major label. You know, that whole sellout thing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 1

podcast.title: "The Rock Show" Van Recovery
podcast.body: A 1980s Dodge van featured in Blink-182's 2001 "The Rock Show" music video disappeared after filming. Andrew Baldwin and Taylor Sheetz, a couple from Texas, became obsessed with finding it and successfully tracked it down to a body shop in Sacramento, California, through online sleuthing and Google Street View. The van had previously been an unclaimed radio station contest prize, then used by a woman named Michelle Delsob and her daughter for guitar practice and parties, before ending up rusted in the auto body shop's yard. The couple purchased it for $1,000, shipped it to Austin for $1,300, and began restoring it. "If you remember that video, it features a Dodge Van for the 1980s that disappeared after they were done shooting the music video."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: StarsNCarsNRockNRoll

podcast.title: 21st Century Reunion
podcast.body: Blink-182 was listed among the alt-rock bands that reunited in the 21st century, a trend that helped to inject a temporary burst of energy into the music scene and reconnect with long-time fans. "In addition, the Pixies...blink 182...These reunions injected some life into the scene, albeit temporary life."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 00s Part 4: Variety Returns

podcast.title: Backstage Rider – Entertainment and Reading Material
podcast.body: Blink-182's rider specified a need for various entertainment items, including DVDs to watch, a selection of current magazines covering fashion, home decor, cars, and science. Additionally, it explicitly requested at least one "X-rated lesbian theme magazine." "at least one had to be, and I quote, an X-rated lesbian theme magazine."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Backstage Rider

podcast.title: Band Bureaucracy Challenges
podcast.body: During the recording of their "Neighborhoods" album, the band faced significant bureaucratic challenges. While they were apart, each member had acquired their own manager, lawyers, accountants, and publicists. At one point, the three-piece band collectively had four managers, making decision-making and project coordination incredibly difficult. "At one point during the recording of neighborhoods, this three-piece band had four managers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 3

podcast.title: Barbecue Band
podcast.body: Blink-182 was once a "Barbecue Band" on the Warped Tour, meaning they prepared post-show meals for other performers and crew in exchange for a slot on the tour. "Barbecue bands have included Blink-1ity-2, Katie Perry, and My Chemical Romance."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: 24 Years of the Warped Tour

podcast.title: Blink-182 Name Change Origin
podcast.body: To resolve the legal dispute with the Irish band also named Blink, the San Diego band agreed to append their name with the number 182. While popular myths link the number to movie references (like the F-bomb count in "Scarface" or the film "Turk-182"), the band maintains that the number "means nothing." "The truth is the number means nothing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 1

podcast.title: Blink-182 Name Formatting
podcast.body: For correct spelling, the band's name should be written with a lowercase 'b' for Blink and a hyphen between "Blink" and "182." Early versions of the "Cheshire Cat" album credited to just "Blink" (without "182") are considered collectible due to this eventual name change. "This means that if you want something collectible, look for early versions of the Cheshire Cat album credited to just Blink and not Blink 182."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 1

podcast.title: Bootlegging of Cheshire Cat
podcast.body: Due to enterprising fans creating and distributing CD burns of the cassette version of "Cheshire Cat," Cargo Records was compelled to release an official CD version of the album. "They had to put out the CD because enterprising fans started bootling the cassette as CD burns."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 1

podcast.title: California New Punk Scene
podcast.body: Blink-182 is mentioned as a band that emerged years later from the "new punk" bases being laid in California in the late 1980s. "bastante años más tardes saldrían pues Blin 182."

podcast.title: Career Trajectory (Late 90s/Early 2000s)

podcast.title: Continued Activity in 2010s
podcast.body: This established band continued its characteristic musical output throughout the 2010s, contrasting with the softer pop alt-rock trend. "Older groups, the food fighters, Lincoln Park, Black Keys, Chili Peppers, Green Day, Queens of the Stone Age, Royal Blood, Muse, Blink 182, Pearl Jam, they just kept doing what they did best."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 2: The Role of Indie Rock

podcast.title: Continued Popularity Post-90s
podcast.body: Blink 182 is one of the acts from the 90s that continued to be very popular, making it difficult for new artists to break through in the 21st century due to their continued demand and airplay.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Theories, Thoughts, and Half-Baked Ideas

podcast.title: Continued Superstar Status
podcast.body: By the close of the 2000s, Blink-182 remained a "superstar act," consistently attracting large audiences. The band also continued to tour into the 2010s. "only the superstar acts like Green Day and Blink 182 continued to draw huge crowds."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: History of Pop Punk: Part 2

podcast.title: Creative Struggles and Label Pressure (Early 2000s)
podcast.body: After "Enema of the State," the band faced significant internal tensions and creative struggles. Their record label pressured them to continue producing pop punk hits, leading to rebellion from the band members who desired to explore new sounds. "This did set up tensions within the band. Call it creative struggles if you want."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 2

podcast.title: Dislike of Reality TV Presence
podcast.body: Tom Delonge expressed his disapproval of Travis Barker's involvement in reality television, specifically the MTV show "Meet the Barkers," which extensively documented Travis and his wife Shannon Mochler. The presence of TV cameras, even in the Blink-182 rehearsal space, was a source of discomfort for Tom. "Tom also wasn't a fan of Travis getting into the reality TV show game."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 3

podcast.title: Donna's Domain Review
podcast.body: Mark Hoppus was described as a "hit with the ladies for obvious reasons" on Donna's Domain, a website that rates rock stars' penis size and sexual ability. This suggests a highly favorable assessment of his attractiveness or performance in the categories rated by the site. "Mark Hopis of Blink 182 is a hit with the ladies for obvious reasons."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: I Did Not Know That

podcast.title: Early 2000s Success and Decline
podcast.body: By 2000, Blink 182 had reached the top, selling albums by the tens of millions, but subsequently faced a career nose dive. "By 2000, they'd made it to the top and were selling albums by the tens of millions."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 2

podcast.title: Early Digital Distribution Experiment
podcast.body: "What's My Age Again?" was part of a pioneering digital distribution experiment in 1999. Thirty-second clips of the song, along with two others, were made available online through a company called A to B music, which was considered "pretty radical stuff back then." "Thirty-second clips of that song and two others were available to anyone online in 1999. Pretty radical stuff back then."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 1

podcast.title: Early Group Names
podcast.body: Before adopting the name Blink, the band was known by several other names, including Duck Tape and Figure Eight, along with other names that have since been forgotten. "The band, which was called Duck Tape and Figure Eight and some other forgotten names, put together a demo tape that they ended up calling Fly Swatter."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 1

podcast.title: Enduring Popularity (Post-90s)
podcast.body: Blink-182 is mentioned as one of the acts from the 1990s that has maintained its popularity and never went away, contributing to the saturated market that makes it challenging for new artists to break through in the 21st century. "Green Day, Blink-182, Chili Peppers, Pearl Jam, Smashing Pumpkins, Food Fighters, even bands that ceased to exist, Stone Temple Pilots, Nirvana, Beastie Boys, for example, continued to be extremely popular with fans."

podcast.title: Enema of the State Album Cover Model
podcast.body: The woman featured on the cover of the "Enema of the State" album is Janine Lindemueller, who was a prominent porn star at the time. The band claimed they were unaware of her identity, stating they simply chose her photo from a stack of options to depict a "sexy nurse" character suitable for the album's title. "The woman on the cover of Enema of the State is Janine Lindemueller. She was a major porn star at the time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 1

podcast.title: Enema of the State Cover Art Censorship
podcast.body: The "Enema of the State" album cover underwent three different versions due to regulatory issues. The initial version featured a red cross on Lindemueller's hat and a capitalized 'B' in "Blink." The 'B' was corrected to lowercase, and subsequently, the American Red Cross intervened, citing the use of their symbol as a violation of the Geneva Convention, leading to its complete removal in the third and final version of the cover. "The American red cross saw the album and said using the red cross symbol in any other way than to signify the world of the real red cross is a violation of the Geneva convention."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 1

podcast.title: Evolution of Sound (Self-Titled Album)
podcast.body: For their self-titled 2003 album, the band sought to grow beyond "goofy adolescent" songs. Influenced by their side projects, Tom and Travis brought a new attitude to Blink 182, resulting in a more experimental, darker, and mature sound. "Like all musicians, they wanted to grow."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 2

podcast.title: Filter Records Dispute
podcast.body: An issue arose concerning Filter Records, the label founded by Mark Hoppas's boss with his savings, leading to a legal dispute over the ownership rights of the early demo tapes that were released through the label. "Now that would later be an issue when there was a dispute over who actually owned these tapes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 1

podcast.title: From Zero to Worldwide Superstars
podcast.body: The band experienced a rapid ascent from obscurity to becoming worldwide superstars, selling 35 million records, before facing significant internal and external challenges that nearly brought them "back to zero again," requiring them to "claw back." "These guys went from zero to worldwide superstars, and then almost back to zero again before clawing back."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: In-Depth History Coverage
podcast.body: Blink-182 was among the specific performers profiled in-depth by the ongoing history program. "In-depth history is on bands like...Blink-182."

srcs.episode: The 500th Show!

podcast.title: Influence on Pop Punk
podcast.body: Blink-182 is considered one of the most influential pop punk bands of the 21st century. Their style and career trajectory have left a significant mark on numerous artists across the genre, inspiring bands like Sum 41, Good Charlotte, Simple Plan, Panic! At The Disco, Fall Out Boy, Hedley, Billy Talent, You Me At Six, and Paramore. "Blink has to be considered one of the most influential pop punk bands of the 21st century."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 3

podcast.title: Jerry Finn's Production Influence
podcast.body: Jerry Finn, who had previously produced Green Day's "Ducky" album, produced Blink-182's "Enema of the State." He brought a wealth of new studio knowledge to the band, significantly influencing their sound at a pivotal time when pop punk was gaining widespread popularity. "He brought in a ton of studio knowledge that was all new to the band and pop punk had become a real thing with fans."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 1

podcast.title: Jerry Finn's Push for Other Projects
podcast.body: Longtime producer Jerry Finn, along with Mark Hoppus and Travis Barker, made it clear they wanted to work on another project during Blink-182's hiatus. This desire led to the formation of Plus 44 by Mark and Travis, further solidifying the band's fragmentation. "It also didn't help the situation that the other two thirds of the band and their long time producer Jerry Finn made it very clear that they wanted to work together on another project."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 3

podcast.title: Manager Rick DeVoe
podcast.body: The band secured Rick DeVoe as their manager, a professional who also managed groups like The Offspring, No Effects, and Pennywise, and who played a significant role in elevating Blink's profile, particularly within the snowboard crowd. "The band attracted a manager, a guy by the name of Rick DeVoe, who also worked with groups like The Offspring and No Effects in Pennywise."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 1

podcast.title: Mark Hoppus's Isolation During Side Projects
podcast.body: While Tom DeLonge and Travis Barker pursued side projects like Box Car Racer and The Transplants, Mark Hoppus "stayed on the sidelines quietly fuming," feeling betrayed that Tom had asked Travis to drum for Box Car Racer, a project that had an "old DIY vibe of early Blink." "Mark left the studio and wrote what he thought would be an instant rejection."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 2

podcast.title: Mark Hoppus's Self-Reflection
podcast.body: Bass player Mark Hoppus once expressed feeling that, despite being in his 20s, he was "still acting like a dumb teenager," reflecting the juvenile and goofy attitude often associated with pop punk. He reportedly "felt bad about that." "Base player Mark Hopper realized that he was in his 20s, but he was still acting like a dumb teenager. He felt bad about that."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: History of Pop Punk: Part 2

podcast.title: Matt Skiba's Film Cameo
podcast.body: Matt Skiba, a member of Blink 182, made an appearance as an extra in the movie "The Dark Knight." "Matt Skiba of Blink 182 can be seen playing an extra in the Dark Knight."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: 60 Mind-Blowing Facts in 60 Minutes: 4th Edition

podcast.title: Meticulous Recording Process (Self-Titled Album)
podcast.body: The recording sessions for the self-titled album were prolonged and exceptionally meticulous. The band tried over 70 different guitars, 30 different amplifiers, at least six drum kits, and rotated 40 different snare drums. They incorporated unusual instruments like Polynesian Camel and Bals, turntables for scratching/looping, old organs, and cellos. An engineer who worked on Pink Floyd's "The Wall" was hired to experiment with various microphones and mic placement techniques. "They were also very, very picky when it came to recording each sound."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 2

podcast.title: Millennium Falcon Van
podcast.body: After accumulating enough funds from their gigs, the band was able to purchase their own van, which they playfully named the "Millennium Falcon." "They soon had enough money to buy their own van, which they dubbed the Millennium Falcon."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 1

podcast.title: Multi-Million Album Sales
podcast.body: In the early 2000s, Blink 182 was highly successful, selling albums by the tens of millions. "Blink 182 was selling albums by the tens of millions."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Multiple Versions of "Enema of the State" Cover
podcast.body: Blink-182's "Enema of the State" album had four different cover versions due to various issues and complaints. The initial version featured a Red Cross on Jeanine Lindemulder's hat and a capital "B" for the band's logo, which was corrected to a lowercase "b" in the second version. Following a complaint from the American Red Cross regarding logo infringement, a third version was released with a plain white nurse's hat. A fourth, censored version, exclusive to Malaysia, removed Lindemulder's cleavage and edited the semi-nude band shot on the back, but oddly brought back the Red Cross symbol. "Anyway, there were actually four different versions of the cover."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Musical Lineage from Green Day
podcast.body: The sound of Blink-182 is described as having descended from Green Day, indicating a clear influence and evolution of a particular punk-pop style. This connection highlights the cyclical nature of musical trends. "And wasn't Blink Sound descended from Green Day?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What A Drag It Is Getting Old (Musically)

podcast.title: Nudity in "What's My Age Again?" Video
podcast.body: The music video for "What's My Age Again?" depicted the band members running around Los Angeles appearing naked, though they were actually wearing flesh-colored speedos. The band later expressed dissatisfaction with this image, aiming to avoid being typecast as a "joke band" or compared to the Red Hot Chili Peppers, and vowed to take more creative control over their public image. "They wanted to leave nudity to the Red Hot Chili Peppers, and they did not want to be viewed as a joke band, so they vowed to take more creative control when it came to their public image."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 1

podcast.title: Origin of "Enema of the State" Title
podcast.body: Blink-182's 1999 album was initially intended to be titled "Turn Your Head and Cough." However, photographer Dave Goldman's spontaneous suggestion to include a rubber glove in the cover art, due to its humorous and suggestive implications, inspired the band to change the album's title to "Enema of the State." "The album was originally going to be called Turn Your Head and Cough, but Goldman suddenly came up with the idea of a glove because he thought that the visual and its implications was pretty funny."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Stories Behind Iconic Album Covers Part 2

podcast.title: Original Name Dispute with Irish Band
podcast.body: The band, initially known simply as "Blink," encountered a legal challenge over their name from an Irish band that had used the same name since recording new tracks in June 1991, predating the San Diego band's usage by several months and also having music available for sale earlier. "Back in June of 1991, an Irish band, who used to go with the name Red and Dino, recorded some new tracks under the name Blink."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 1

podcast.title: Pennywise's Financial Support
podcast.body: When Blink-182 received an invitation to perform in Australia but lacked the necessary funds for travel, the members of the band Pennywise stepped in and purchased their plane tickets. "So the guys in the band Pennywise bought them their tickets."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 1

podcast.title: Pop Punk Decline (2010s)
podcast.body: Despite the general decline of pop punk in the early 2010s, Blink 182, among other bands, persisted in the genre. However, the band, considered one of the biggest pop punk acts, started to "sputter," contributing to the decline of the genre. "Blink 1.82, one of the biggest of all the pop punk bands, if not the biggest, had started to really sputter."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 2: The Role of Indie Rock

podcast.title: Pop Punk Heritage Act
podcast.body: Blink-182 was identified as one of the "Big Heritage Acts" of Pop Punk that kept the spirit of the genre alive in the 2010s, despite its popularity being nowhere near its 90s or 2000s peaks. There was also a sentiment in some punk circles to reclaim punk from "Corporatized Punk" exemplified by bands like Blink-182. "The Big Heritage Acts were still there, you know, offspring, link quantity to some 41 simple plan, and they kept the spirit alive." "There's also the sense in some quarters that Punk needs to be torn down and rebuilt, reclaimed from the so-called Croppered Punk, exemplified by Blink-Wentety 2-Some41 in the offspring."

srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 4: The Revivals

podcast.title: Popularity and Green Day Support (Late 1990s)
podcast.body: The band was "really hot at the time" and provided an opening tour slot for Green Day, which helped to save Green Day from breaking up. "Blink was really hot at the time..."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 14

podcast.title: Post-Breakup Reunion
podcast.body: Blink-182 managed to resolve their internal differences and eventually reunited, joining a significant wave of bands from various eras who got back together in the 21st century. This reunion trend was often driven by the financial opportunities presented by live touring amidst declining CD sales. "Blink-182 eventually sorted things out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 1: (100-91)

podcast.title: Post-Revival Success
podcast.body: Blink 182 was one of the few punk bands that continued to experience significant success after the initial peak of the mid-90s punk rock revival (1994-1996), becoming one of the biggest American bands globally by the end of the decade. "The punk rock revival of the 90s peaked through 1994 to 1996 before a rand of gas with the exceptions of a few bands. Green Day, offspring, Blink 1-2."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 90s Part 6: The Punk Revival

podcast.title: Post-Take Off Your Pants and Jacket Break
podcast.body: After fulfilling obligations for "Take Off Your Pants and Jacket," the band desperately needed a break due to intense pressure and internal tensions. Tom DeLonge also had serious back issues, including a herniated disc requiring surgery, necessitating time off from Blink 182. "They desperately needed some time apart."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 2

podcast.title: Recurring Sound Patterns
podcast.body: The recurring similarity between new songs by Blink-182 and their older material is a common observation among listeners, suggesting a consistent stylistic approach over time. "How many times have you said, hey, that new song by Blink sounds a lot like the song by Blink from back in the day?"

podcast.title: Ringtone Popularity - Mid-2000s
podcast.body: In the mid-2000s, songs by artists like Blink-182 were constantly heard as ringtones in public spaces such as the subway, schools, hospitals, and streets. This reflected a widespread desire among young people to publicly display their musical tastes and individuality. "Canciones de Metallica, Eminem, Fifth Dissent, Blint Note, Linkin Park, The Vanessens, sonaban constantemente en el metro, en el colegio, en el hospital, en la calle."

podcast.title: San Diego Skate Park Origins
podcast.body: The band's early activities and formation were deeply rooted in the skate park suburbs of San Diego, a region identified as a hub where music began "brewing" that would ultimately lead to 35 million records sold. podcast.title: Saving Green Day (Pop Disaster Tour)
podcast.body: Blink 182 joined Green Day on the Pop Disaster Tour, a pairing intended as a last-ditch effort to revitalize Green Day's career, which seemed to be on the decline. The tour successfully introduced Green Day to a new, younger audience and forced Blink 182 to improve their live performances. "So Blink 182 saved Green Day."

podcast.title: Scott Rainer's Broken Heels
podcast.body: During the recording sessions for "Dude Ranch," drummer Scott Rainer, under the influence of alcohol, believed he could fly and jumped off an unspecified object, resulting in him breaking both his heels. Consequently, he recorded most of his drum parts while in a wheelchair or on crutches. "One night Scott got a little drunk and was convinced he could fly. So he jumped off something and broke both his heels."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 1

podcast.title: Sleeping Arrangements during Cheshire Cat Recording
podcast.body: During the six-day recording sessions for "Cheshire Cat," the band members conserved resources by staying in a single hotel room that contained only one king-size bed, forcing them to sleep "three across" for a few hours each night. "They stayed at a hotel down the street in a room with exactly one king-size bed. So they slept a few hours each night, sleeping three across."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 1

podcast.title: Surviving Multiple Lifespans
podcast.body: Despite the general observation that bands have an average lifespan of seven years, Blink-182 has defied this trend, navigating through several such cycles of career highs, lows, and lineup changes. "Blink 182 has gone through several of those lifetimes."

podcast.title: Tens of Millions in Album Sales
podcast.body: The band achieved significant commercial success, selling "tens of millions of albums" during their initial run. "After a good run in tens of millions of albums, Blink 182 started to fracture."

srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Tom DeLong's Financial Difficulties
podcast.body: Tom DeLong and his wife faced financial troubles due to the US housing bust, trying to sell their large 6500 sq ft, 5-bathroom house in Rancho Santa Fe, California (1.1 acres in a gated community), initially listed at $8 million, then $6.25 million, and finally $5.1 million, resulting in an estimated 20% loss after renovations. "Tom DeLong and his wife have been caught up in the housing bust in the US."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Tom Delonge's Desire for Break
podcast.body: Tom Delonge's decision to take a break stemmed from feeling the intense grind of the band's schedule and needing at least six months to decompress. He was disappointed that Mark Hoppus and Travis Barker didn't fully understand his need for this extended time away. "The story seems to be that Tom just wanted a break from the grind and he was disappointed that the other two guys didn't understand why he needed at least six months to decompress."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 3

podcast.title: Tom Overcomes Addiction
podcast.body: Tom successfully broke his addiction to prescription painkillers by going "cold turkey," an intense experience where he "sweated it out in a room for two weeks hallucinating." "First of all, Tom broke his addiction to prescription pain killers by going cold turkey. He said he sweated it out in a room for two weeks hallucinating."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Tour with Green Day (Later Career)
podcast.body: Later in their career, after achieving sales of tens of millions of records, Blink-182 toured with Green Day, confirming Green Day's "elder statesman" role in the punk community. "And then the next time Green Day went on the road, it was with Blink 1 and 2, who were by this time selling tens of millions of records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: 24 Years of the Warped Tour

podcast.title: Tour with Green Day (early 2000s)
podcast.body: Blink-182, a band then "on the ascendancy," toured with Green Day at a time when Green Day was perceived to be fading by the late 1990s. This tour was a strategic move by Green Day's record label, hoping to leverage Blink-182's rising popularity to rekindle interest in the older band. "And then Green Day went out onto her with Blink 182, a band that was on the ascended."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 5: (60-51)

podcast.title: Touring with Saves the Day
podcast.body: Blink-182 toured with the emo band Saves the Day, alongside Weezer, Green Day, and Dashboard Confessional, showing the integration of emo bands into broader touring circuits with established artists. "Saves the Day, definitely an emo band, toured with not just fellow travelers Weezer, but also Green Day and Blink 182, and Dashboard Confessional, Open for You too."

podcast.title: Travis Barker's Cadillac Obsession
podcast.body: Travis Barker, the drummer for Blink-182, demonstrates a profound love for Cadillacs, evidenced by numerous tattoos and a substantial car collection. His multi-million dollar car collection features several Cadillacs, including a 1965 Deville convertible, a 1960 Coupe Deville, and a 1941 Series 62 Deluxe. xref.title: Career Revival (Circa 2000)

xref.title: "The Rock Show" Van Recovery
xref.body: A 1980s Dodge van featured in Blink-182's 2001 "The Rock Show" music video disappeared after filming. Andrew Baldwin and Taylor Sheetz, a couple from Texas, became obsessed with finding it and successfully tracked it down to a body shop in Sacramento, California, through online sleuthing and Google Street View. The van had previously been an unclaimed radio station contest prize, then used by a woman named Michelle Delsob and her daughter for guitar practice and parties, before ending up rusted in the auto body shop's yard. The couple purchased it for $1,000, shipped it to Austin for $1,300, and began restoring it. xref.body: In July 2008, longtime Blink-182 producer Jerry Finn had just completed his work on a Morrissey album shortly before suffering a cerebral hemorrhage and a massive heart attack, which ultimately led to his death. "In July 2008, just after finishing up work on a Morrissey album, he suffered a cerebral hemorrhage that was followed by a massive heart attack, which destroyed him."

xref.title: Jerry Finn's Production Influence
xref.body: Jerry Finn, who had previously produced Green Day's "Ducky" album, produced Blink-182's "Enema of the State." He brought a wealth of new studio knowledge to the band, significantly influencing their sound at a pivotal time when pop punk was gaining widespread popularity. "He brought in a ton of studio knowledge that was all new to the band and pop punk had become a real thing with fans."

xref.title: Jerry Finn's Push for Other Projects
xref.body: Longtime producer Jerry Finn, along with Mark Hoppus and Travis Barker, made it clear they wanted to work on another project during Blink-182's hiatus. This desire led to the formation of Plus 44 by Mark and Travis, further solidifying the band's fragmentation. "It also didn't help the situation that the other two thirds of the band and their long time producer Jerry Finn made it very clear that they wanted to work together on another project."

xref.title: Multiple Versions of "Enema of the State" Cover
xref.body: Blink-182's "Enema of the State" album had four different cover versions due to various issues and complaints. The initial version featured a Red Cross on Jeanine Lindemulder's hat and a capital "B" for the band's logo, which was corrected to a lowercase "b" in the second version. Following a complaint from the American Red Cross regarding logo infringement, a third version was released with a plain white nurse's hat. A fourth, censored version, exclusive to Malaysia, removed Lindemulder's cleavage and edited the semi-nude band shot on the back, but oddly brought back the Red Cross symbol. "Anyway, there were actually four different versions of the cover."

xref.title: Origin of "Enema of the State" Title
xref.body: Blink-182's 1999 album was initially intended to be titled "Turn Your Head and Cough." However, photographer Dave Goldman's spontaneous suggestion to include a rubber glove in the cover art, due to its humorous and suggestive implications, inspired the band to change the album's title to "Enema of the State." "The album was originally going to be called Turn Your Head and Cough, but Goldman suddenly came up with the idea of a glove because he thought that the visual and its implications was pretty funny."

xref.title: Personal Hardships (2000s)
xref.body: During the mid-2000s, Tom DeLonge faced significant personal challenges. His brother was deployed to Iraq, a war he opposed, and his father was diagnosed with leukemia. These events, combined with the Blink-182 breakup and a serious back injury that led to painkiller addiction, created a difficult period in his life. "His brother was deployed to Iraq, a war that Tom opposed. His father was diagnosed with leukemia. In other words, it wasn't a very good time."

xref.title: Pop Punk Heritage Act
xref.body: Blink-182 was identified as one of the "Big Heritage Acts" of Pop Punk that kept the spirit of the genre alive in the 2010s, despite its popularity being nowhere near its 90s or 2000s peaks. There was also a sentiment in some punk circles to reclaim punk from "Corporatized Punk" exemplified by bands like Blink-182. "The Big Heritage Acts were still there, you know, offspring, link quantity to some 41 simple plan, and they kept the spirit alive." "There's also the sense in some quarters that Punk needs to be torn down and rebuilt, reclaimed from the so-called Croppered Punk, exemplified by Blink-Wentety 2-Some41 in the offspring."
